name: Chapter 9: Biomolecules
description: Chemical analysis of tissues, metabolites, proteins, polysaccharides, nucleic acids and enzymes

cards.term: How does the elemental list of living tissue differ from that of earth's crust?
cards.definition: The same elements are present, but carbon and hydrogen are relatively far more abundant in living organisms

cards.term: Table 9.1: elements in crust vs body
cards.definition: Carbon: 0.03 vs 18.5; Hydrogen: 0.14 vs 9.5; Oxygen: 46.6 vs 65.0; Nitrogen: very little vs 3.3; Silicon: 27.7 vs negligible

cards.term: Which element is most abundant by weight in both the crust and the human body?
cards.definition: Oxygen (46.6% and 65%)

cards.term: In what is living tissue ground for chemical analysis?
cards.definition: Trichloroacetic acid (Cl₃CCOOH)

cards.term: Acid-soluble pool vs acid-insoluble fraction?
cards.definition: Filtrate = acid-soluble pool (small molecules). Retentate = acid-insoluble fraction (macromolecules).

cards.term: What are biomolecules?
cards.definition: All the carbon compounds obtained from living tissues

cards.term: Wet weight, dry weight and ash?
cards.definition: Wet: fresh tissue. Dry: after water evaporates. Ash: what remains after burning; contains inorganic elements (Ca, Mg...).

cards.term: Name the inorganic constituents of living tissue (Table 9.2).
cards.definition: Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, water, and compounds NaCl, CaCO₃, PO₄³⁻, SO₄²⁻

cards.term: What is an α-amino acid?
cards.definition: An amino group and an acidic (carboxyl) group on the same carbon, the α-carbon

cards.term: Name the four groups on the α-carbon of an amino acid.
cards.definition: Hydrogen, carboxyl group, amino group, variable R group

cards.term: How many amino acids occur in proteins?
cards.definition: Twenty

cards.text: R group = hydrogen: {{c1::glycine}}; methyl: {{c2::alanine}}; hydroxy methyl: {{c3::serine}}.

cards.term: Give an acidic, a basic and a neutral amino acid.
cards.definition: Acidic: glutamic acid. Basic: lysine. Neutral: valine.

cards.term: Name the aromatic amino acids.
cards.definition: Tyrosine, phenylalanine, tryptophan

cards.term: What is the zwitterionic form of an amino acid?
cards.definition: The form carrying both a positive (–NH₃⁺) and a negative (–COO⁻) charge; amino acid structure changes with pH because –NH₂ and –COOH ionise

cards.term: Why is the zwitterion called that? (intuition)
cards.definition: German zwitter = hybrid: one molecule, both charges, net charge zero

cards.term: What is a fatty acid?
cards.definition: A carboxyl group attached to an R group (1 to 19 carbons)

cards.term: How many carbons in palmitic acid and arachidonic acid?
cards.definition: Palmitic: 16. Arachidonic: 20 (both including the carboxyl carbon).

cards.term: Saturated vs unsaturated fatty acid?
cards.definition: Saturated: no double bond. Unsaturated: one or more C=C double bonds.

cards.term: What is glycerol?
cards.definition: Trihydroxy propane

cards.term: What are mono-, di- and triglycerides?
cards.definition: Glycerol esterified with one, two or three fatty acids

cards.term: Fats vs oils?
cards.definition: Classified by melting point: oils have a lower melting point and stay liquid in winter (e.g. gingelly oil)

cards.term: What are phospholipids? Example?
cards.definition: Lipids with phosphorus and a phosphorylated organic compound; in cell membranes, e.g. lecithin

cards.term: Name the five nitrogen bases.
cards.definition: Adenine, guanine, cytosine, uracil, thymine

cards.term: Nucleoside vs nucleotide?
cards.definition: Nucleoside = base + sugar. Nucleotide = base + sugar + phosphate.

cards.term: Is adenosine a nucleoside or nucleotide? Adenylic acid?
cards.definition: Adenosine: nucleoside. Adenylic acid: nucleotide.

cards.term: Figure 9.1: which classes of small biomolecules are shown?
cards.definition: Sugars (glucose, ribose), amino acids (glycine, alanine, serine), lipids (fatty acid, glycerol, triglyceride, lecithin, cholesterol), nitrogen bases, nucleosides, nucleotide

cards.term: Purines vs pyrimidines?
cards.definition: Purines: adenine, guanine. Pyrimidines: cytosine, uracil, thymine.

cards.term: Mnemonic for purines?
cards.definition: "Pure As Gold": purines are Adenine and Guanine. (Pyrimidines have the "y": cytosine, thymine, and uracil.)

cards.term: Primary vs secondary metabolites?
cards.definition: Primary: identifiable roles in normal physiology (e.g. amino acids, sugars). Secondary: in plants, fungi, microbes; roles in the host often unknown.

cards.term: Table 9.3: secondary metabolites
cards.definition: Pigments: Carotenoids, anthocyanins; Alkaloids: Morphine, codeine; Terpenoids: Monoterpenes, diterpenes; Essential oils: Lemon grass oil; Toxins: Abrin, ricin; Lectins: Concanavalin A; Drugs: Vinblastin, curcumin; Polymeric substances: Rubber, gums, cellulose

cards.term: Which secondary metabolite is a lectin?
cards.definition: Concanavalin A

cards.term: Name two toxins among secondary metabolites.
cards.definition: Abrin, ricin

cards.term: Molecular weight range in the acid-soluble pool?
cards.definition: 18 to ~800 daltons

cards.term: Name the four organic compound classes of the acid-insoluble fraction.
cards.definition: Proteins, nucleic acids, polysaccharides, lipids

cards.term: Micromolecules vs macromolecules?
cards.definition: Micro: below 1000 Da. Macro: in the acid-insoluble fraction (≥ ~10,000 Da, except lipids).

cards.term: Why do lipids (under 800 Da) appear in the acid-insoluble fraction?
cards.definition: They form membranes; grinding breaks membranes into insoluble vesicles. Lipids are not strictly macromolecules.

cards.term: What does the acid-soluble pool roughly represent?
cards.definition: The cytoplasmic composition

cards.term: Table 9.4: composition of cells
cards.definition: Water: 70–90; Proteins: 10–15; Nucleic acids: 5–7; Carbohydrates: 3; Lipids: 2; Ions: 1

cards.term: Most abundant chemical in living organisms?
cards.definition: Water

cards.term: What are proteins?
cards.definition: Polypeptides: linear chains of amino acids joined by peptide bonds

cards.term: Is a protein a homopolymer or heteropolymer? Why?
cards.definition: Heteropolymer: made of up to 20 different amino acids

cards.term: Essential vs non-essential amino acids?
cards.definition: Essential: must come from the diet. Non-essential: the body can make them.

cards.term: Table 9.5: protein functions
cards.definition: Collagen: Intercellular ground substance; Trypsin: Enzyme; Insulin: Hormone; Antibody: Fights infectious agents; Receptor: Sensory reception (smell, taste, hormone); GLUT-4: Glucose transport into cells

cards.term: Most abundant protein in the animal world? In the whole biosphere?
cards.definition: Animals: collagen. Biosphere: RuBisCO (Ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase-oxygenase).

cards.term: What are polysaccharides?
cards.definition: Long chains of sugars (monosaccharide building blocks)

cards.term: Monomer of cellulose? Homo- or heteropolymer?
cards.definition: Glucose; a homopolymer

cards.term: Storage polysaccharide in plants vs animals?
cards.definition: Plants: starch. Animals: glycogen.

cards.term: Inulin is a polymer of which sugar?
cards.definition: Fructose

cards.term: Which end of a glycogen chain is reducing?
cards.definition: The right end (left = non-reducing)

cards.term: Why does starch turn blue with iodine but cellulose does not?
cards.definition: Starch forms helical secondary structures that hold I₂; cellulose has no complex helices

cards.term: What is chitin, and where is it found?
cards.definition: A complex polysaccharide of amino-sugars; in the exoskeletons of arthropods (and fungal walls)

cards.term: What are complex polysaccharides built from?
cards.definition: Amino-sugars and modified sugars, e.g. glucosamine, N-acetyl galactosamine

cards.term: Three components of a nucleotide?
cards.definition: A heterocyclic nitrogenous base, a monosaccharide, and phosphate

cards.term: Which three kinds of macromolecules make the true macromolecular fraction?
cards.definition: Polysaccharides, polypeptides, polynucleotides

cards.term: Sugar in DNA vs RNA?
cards.definition: DNA: 2'-deoxyribose. RNA: ribose.

cards.term: What is the primary structure of a protein?
cards.definition: The sequence of amino acids

cards.term: N-terminal vs C-terminal amino acid?
cards.definition: N-terminal: the first amino acid (left). C-terminal: the last (right).

cards.term: Which helices are found in proteins?
cards.definition: Only right-handed helices

cards.term: What is tertiary structure, and why does it matter?
cards.definition: The chain folded on itself like a hollow woollen ball: the 3-D shape, essential for biological activity

cards.term: What is quaternary structure? Example?
cards.definition: Arrangement of several subunits, e.g. adult haemoglobin: 2 α + 2 β

cards.term: Figure 9.3 · Levels of protein structure
Are all enzymes proteins?
cards.definition: Almost all; some nucleic acids act as enzymes: ribozymes

cards.term: What is the active site?
cards.definition: A crevice or pocket in the folded enzyme into which the substrate fits

cards.term: Enzymes vs inorganic catalysts: temperature?
cards.definition: Inorganic catalysts work at high temperature and pressure; enzymes are damaged above ~40 °C (except those of thermophiles, stable up to 80–90 °C)

cards.term: Physical change vs chemical reaction?
cards.definition: Physical: shape or state changes without breaking bonds. Chemical: bonds broken and new ones formed.

cards.term: Rate of a reaction?
cards.definition: Amount of product per unit time: rate \(= \dfrac{\delta P}{\delta t}\)

cards.term: Rule of thumb: temperature and reaction rate?
cards.definition: Rate doubles (or halves) for every 10 °C change

cards.term: How much does carbonic anhydrase speed up CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃?
cards.definition: From ~200 molecules/hour to ~600,000/second: about 10 million times

cards.term: What is a metabolic pathway?
cards.definition: A multistep reaction, each step catalysed by the same enzyme complex or different enzymes

cards.term: Glucose → pyruvic acid takes how many enzyme steps?
cards.definition: Ten

cards.term: End product of the glucose pathway in muscle (anaerobic), aerobic cells, and yeast?
cards.definition: Muscle, anaerobic: lactic acid. Aerobic: pyruvic acid. Yeast fermentation: ethanol.

cards.term: NCERT writes glucose → pyruvate with O₂. Does glycolysis need oxygen? (clarification)
cards.definition: No. Glycolysis itself is anaerobic. The O₂ in NCERT's overall equation re-oxidises the NADH formed; the ten steps run without oxygen.

cards.term: What is the ES complex?
cards.definition: The transient complex formed when the substrate binds the enzyme's active site; its formation is obligatory for catalysis

cards.term: What is the transition state?
cards.definition: An unstable, high-energy structure the substrate passes through on its way to product

cards.term: What is activation energy?
cards.definition: The difference in energy between the substrate and the transition state

cards.term: How do enzymes speed up reactions?
cards.definition: By lowering the activation energy

cards.term: If product P is at a lower energy than S, the reaction is...?
cards.definition: Exothermic (no need to supply heat)

cards.term: Figure 9.4 · Concept of activation energy

cards.text: Catalytic cycle: E + S → {{c1::ES}} → {{c2::EP}} → E + P.

cards.term: List the four steps of the catalytic cycle.
cards.definition:
1. Substrate binds the active site
  2. Binding makes the enzyme change shape, fitting tighter (induced fit)
  3. Active site breaks bonds; EP complex forms
  4. Product released; enzyme free again

cards.term: Which factors affect enzyme activity?
cards.definition: Temperature, pH, substrate concentration, binding of specific chemicals (by altering tertiary structure)

cards.term: Effect of low vs high temperature on enzymes?
cards.definition: Low: enzyme temporarily inactive (preserved). High: denatured, activity destroyed.

cards.term: What are optimum temperature and pH?
cards.definition: The temperature and pH at which an enzyme shows its highest activity

cards.term: Why does reaction velocity level off at Vmax as [S] rises?
cards.definition: All enzyme molecules are saturated with substrate; none free for more substrate

cards.term: What is Km (Figure 9.5 c)? (beyond NCERT text)
cards.definition: The substrate concentration at which velocity is half of Vmax; a low Km means high affinity

cards.term: What is a competitive inhibitor?
cards.definition: A chemical that resembles the substrate and competes for the substrate-binding site

cards.term: Classic example of competitive inhibition?
cards.definition: Malonate inhibits succinic dehydrogenase (resembles succinate)

cards.term: Where are competitive inhibitors used?
cards.definition: In controlling bacterial pathogens

cards.term: How many classes of enzymes? How are they numbered?
cards.definition: Six classes, each with 4–13 subclasses, named by a four-digit number

cards.term: Six enzyme classes
cards.definition: Oxidoreductases: Oxidoreduction between two substrates; Transferases: Transfer of a group (not H) between substrates; Hydrolases: Hydrolysis of ester, ether, peptide, glycosidic, C–C, C–halide, P–N bonds; Lyases: Removal of groups by non-hydrolytic means, leaving double bonds; Isomerases: Inter-conversion of optical, geometric, positional isomers; Ligases: Joining two compounds (C–O, C–S, C–N, P–O bonds)

cards.term: Mnemonic for the six enzyme classes, in order?
cards.definition: "Over The Hill, Lazy Iguanas Lounge": Oxidoreductases, Transferases, Hydrolases, Lyases, Isomerases, Ligases

cards.term: What is an apoenzyme?
cards.definition: The protein part of an enzyme that needs a cofactor

cards.term: Name the three kinds of cofactors.
cards.definition: Prosthetic groups, co-enzymes, metal ions

cards.term: Prosthetic group vs co-enzyme?
cards.definition: Both organic. Prosthetic group: tightly bound. Co-enzyme: transient association during catalysis.

cards.term: Example of a prosthetic group?
cards.definition: Haem in peroxidase and catalase (break down H₂O₂)

cards.term: Which vitamin is part of NAD and NADP?
cards.definition: Niacin

cards.term: Which metal ion is a cofactor for carboxypeptidase?
cards.definition: Zinc

cards.term: What happens if the cofactor is removed?
cards.definition: Catalytic activity is lost
